title: Detection of Social Media
summary: This detection strategy covers reconnaissance through social media, the technique where an adversary reads public profiles, posts, job adverts and group discussions to learn who works at a target, what tools the staff use and how the organisation is structured. It matters because this collection creates no log on the victim estate, so the only practical signals are on the defender's own browsing and identity side: staff accounts reaching social platforms from corporate addresses, bulk profile viewing, saved searches on competitor names, and newly registered or freshly created accounts that immediately search for employees. The telemetry that makes it possible is web proxy and secure web gateway records with the requested host, the full uniform resource locator, the user agent and the authenticated user, joined with single sign on and human resources directory data. Detection fails in practice because social platforms are legitimate work tools for recruiting, sales and marketing teams, so the rule must separate casual business use from systematic employee enumeration by one account.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for unusual use of social media from company devices. It watches for one account reading many staff profiles in a short time. The alert points to possible information gathering before an attack.
beginner.whyItMatters: Social pages often list names, roles, email addresses and the software a team uses. An attacker can collect all of that without touching your network. Nothing is broken, so no alarm sounds on your servers. Watching your own side is the only way to notice the collection.
howItWorks: User web traffic passes through a proxy, which records the site, the full address and the signed in user.
Those proxy records are sent to your security monitoring platform, called a security information and event management system.
The rule selects traffic to known social and business networking sites and keeps the profile and search paths.
It counts profile views and search requests per user in a short window, for example one hour.
It compares that count with the normal pattern for the user, the team and the time of day.
A high count, especially from a newly created account or an unusual device, raises an alert for review.
beginner.example: Think of a person sitting in a public library reading the staff notice board. The board is open to everyone, so nobody calls the police. However, a visitor who writes down every name and every job title is not reading for fun. This detection watches how many names one visitor copies.
takeaways: Social media collection happens off your network, so watch your own users instead.
One profile view is normal, but hundreds from one account is a signal worth reviewing.
Always baseline the recruiting and sales teams, because their work looks the same.

objectives: Explain how public social media content supports later targeting and phishing.
Name the proxy and identity fields that attribute this activity to a real person.
Write a threshold rule that counts profile and search requests per account.
Describe how to profile recruiting and marketing users before setting a threshold.
Explain why this activity rarely appears in endpoint or server logs.
dataSources: Secure web gateway and proxy logs with the requested host, full uniform resource locator, authenticated user and user agent
Single sign on authentication records showing which corporate account opened the social platform session
Human resources directory data mapping staff to teams, roles and start dates for baseline comparison
Domain name system query logs from corporate resolvers showing lookups of social and business networking domains
logic: The pattern is one corporate identity reaching social and business networking hosts far more often than its peers within a short window, where the requested paths are profile pages, people searches or saved searches rather than a single feed page, and where the account, device or user agent is new for that identity. The fields that must be correlated are the authenticated user, the requested host and path, the request count per window, the user agent and device, and the team baseline from the previous thirty days. The benign case is a recruiter or sales person browsing profiles as part of normal work, which is stable over weeks and spread through the working day; the malicious case is a burst of profile views by an account that normally never touches these sites, often combined with directory lookups and mail address collection.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk Social Media Profile Access by Corporate Account
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: web_proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'linkedin.com/in/'
#       - 'facebook.com/'
#       - 'x.com/'
#     http_method: 'GET'
#   filter_business:
#     user|endswith:
#       - 'recruiting'
#       - 'sales'
#   condition: selection and not filter_business | count() by user > 150 within 1h
# level: low
falsePositives: Recruiters and talent teams who review hundreds of candidate profiles during a hiring drive
Sales and partnership staff who research named contacts before a customer meeting
Marketing staff who monitor brand mentions and competitor pages throughout the day
An employee who uses a social platform for a personal project during a lunch break
tuningNotes: Start by measuring the daily profile request count per user for thirty days and set the threshold above the ninety fifth percentile of the recruiting and sales groups, then scope the high severity version to accounts outside those groups. Add a filter for known personal devices on the guest wireless network, because that traffic is not a corporate session. Filter out requests that carry a mobile application user agent, since the mobile feed generates many profile hits from one scroll. Keep a low severity version for everyone so that slow collection over days is still visible, because a tight threshold on one hour will miss an adversary who reads ten profiles a day for a month.
